design_detail: Phase 2, double-blind, doubly randomized, delayed-start, placebo-controlled trial (a variant of the sequential parallel comparison design) of intranasal esketamine (the S-enantiomer of ketamine), panel A of the SYNAPSE study, at 14 outpatient sites (13 in the USA, 1 in Belgium), 28 January 2014 to 25 September 2015, sponsored by Janssen Research & Development. 67 adults with DSM-IV-TR major depressive disorder and treatment-resistant depression (inadequate response to 2 or more antidepressants, at least 1 in the current episode) continued their oral antidepressant unchanged. Period 1 (days 1 to 8): randomized 3:1:1:1 to placebo spray (33) or esketamine 28 mg (11), 56 mg (11) or 84 mg (12) on days 1 and 4. Period 2 (days 8 to 15): the 28 placebo-treated participants with moderate or severe symptoms (QIDS-SR16 of 11 or more) were rerandomized 1:1:1:1 (placebo 6, 28 mg 8, 56 mg 9, 84 mg 5) for days 8 and 11; the others stayed on placebo. Then optional open-label esketamine (days 15 to 74, flexible 28 to 84 mg, twice weekly for 2 weeks, weekly for 3 weeks, then every 2 weeks) and 8 weeks of follow-up without esketamine. Primary end point: MADRS change from each period's baseline to its day 8 (ANCOVA), the two periods combined by a weighted test. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01998958.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with treatment-resistant depression who continued an oral antidepressant, twice-weekly esketamine nasal spray at 28, 56 or 84 mg for 1 week lowered clinician-rated depression (MADRS) more than a bitter-tasting placebo spray, whether the difference rose with dose, and which adverse effects, blood-pressure rises and dissociative symptoms followed dosing over 2 weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether improvement lasts or is maintained by less frequent dosing (the open-label and follow-up phases had no control group and were analysed in those still present, all on their oral antidepressant); the effect without the oral antidepressant or against racemic ketamine; whether blinding held (not assessed); effects in people with psychotic features, PTSD, OCD, a substance or alcohol use disorder in the past year, recent cannabis use or suicidal intent (excluded); or rare and long-term harms (56 people given esketamine double-blind for at most 2 weeks, 57 in the open-label phase).

sample.recruitment: Multiple outpatient referral centres (14 sites); 126 screened and 67 randomized; financial compensation was provided. How participants were found is not described in the main text (Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants; Methods › Population, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Design, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Medically stable adults aged 20 to 64 with DSM-IV-TR major depressive disorder; treatment-resistant depression defined as inadequate response to 2 or more antidepressants on the Massachusetts General Hospital Antidepressant Treatment Response Questionnaire, at least 1 in the current episode (a failure in a prior episode otherwise acceptable); IDS-C30 of 34 or more at screening and before the day-1 dose. Excluded: recent or current suicidal ideation with intent to act, suicidal behaviour, homicidal ideation or intent, bipolar and related disorders, intellectual disability, psychotic disorder, MDD with psychosis, PTSD, OCD, substance or alcohol use disorder in the past year and recent cannabis use; further criteria only in the eAppendix (not read) (Methods › Population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: 38 women of 67; mean age 44.7 (SD 10.0). In the current episode 43 (64%) reported only 1 antidepressant failure (plus 1 in an earlier episode), 15 (22%) 2 and 9 (13%) 3 or more; 26 (39%) had used an atypical antipsychotic as add-on treatment before entry. Other characteristics, by arm, only in eTable 3 (not read); race and ethnicity not given in the main text (Abstract › Results; Results › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: 63 of 67 (94%) completed period 1 and 60 of 67 (90%) both double-blind periods; 57 entered the open-label phase, 51 (89%) of them the follow-up phase, and 41 (80% of those) completed the week-8 follow-up visit. Discontinuations by arm are given only in Figure 1, an image not extracted. Adverse events led to stopping in 3 of 56 esketamine-treated participants in the double-blind phase, none on placebo, and 1 of 57 in the open-label phase (Results › Participants, 1st paragraph; Results › Safety, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Sponsor-run outpatient sites with paid participation and strict exclusions (suicidal intent, PTSD, OCD, recent substance or cannabis use). The definition of treatment resistance is broad: 64% had failed only one antidepressant in the current episode. The period-2 sample is selected for non-response to placebo. Results apply to esketamine added to an ongoing oral antidepressant.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug in disposable nasal spray devices of 200 μL (2 sprays): each 100-μL spray delivered esketamine hydrochloride 16.14 (unit not printed; 14 mg of esketamine base) or placebo (water for injection with the bittering agent denatonium benzoate to mimic the taste). On each double-blind dosing day participants self-administered study drug at 3 time points 5 minutes apart whatever their dose group; in the open-label phase at 1, 2 or 3 time points for 28, 56 or 84 mg (Methods › Study Drug and Administration). No blood levels are reported in this article.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: double-blind esketamine 28, 56 or 84 mg or placebo by nasal spray on days 1 and 4 (period 1) and days 8 and 11 (period 2); open-label 56 mg on day 15, then 28 to 84 mg at the investigator's judgment, twice weekly for 2 weeks, weekly for 3 weeks, then every 2 weeks to day 74 (7 participants enrolled under the original protocol received only 2 weeks of open-label drug). The oral antidepressant taken before entry continued unchanged throughout (Methods › Design, 3rd paragraph; Study Drug and Administration; Table 2 footnote a).
exposure.polysubstance: Substance or alcohol use disorder in the past year and recent cannabis use excluded; how this was checked, and tobacco or alcohol use, are not reported in the main text (Methods › Population, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: participants continued their prescribed oral antidepressant; recent cannabis use was an exclusion.

comparison.controls: Placebo nasal spray (water with a bittering agent) in identical devices on the same schedule, alongside the same continued oral antidepressant. In period 2, placebo-treated participants with moderate or severe symptoms were rerandomized and the others continued placebo, all going through an identical process to keep the blind (Methods › Design, 3rd paragraph; Study Drug and Administration, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Two computer-generated randomization schedules (period 1 and period 2), randomly permuted blocks, stratified by centre (Methods › Design, 3rd paragraph); how allocation was concealed is not described. Groups described as similar (eTable 3, not read); period-1 baseline MADRS 35.0 (SD 5.18) placebo, 31.3 (3.80) 28 mg, 33.2 (6.26) 56 mg, 35.0 (4.22) 84 mg (Table 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same population; all continued their oral antidepressant.

outcomes.instruments: MADRS (clinician-rated depression, 0 to 60, with the SIGMA structured interview guide) on day 1 before and 2 hours after the dose and on days 2, 8 (before the dose), 9 and 15, and in the open-label and follow-up phases; Clinical Global Impression of Severity; GAD-7 (self-rated anxiety; results only in eTables 1 and 2, not read); QIDS-SR16 for rerandomization. Response: a MADRS fall of 50% or more; remission: MADRS of 10 or less. Safety: adverse events throughout; laboratory tests, vital signs and examination at set times; vital signs, the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale (CADSS, dissociation) and the 4-item BPRS positive symptom subscale (psychotic-type symptoms) before the dose and 40 minutes and 2 hours after it (Methods › Efficacy Assessments; Safety Assessments; Table 2 footnote c). The 2-hour MADRS falls at the end of the acute effects, which the article says resolved by 2 hours; the primary end point (day 8) falls 4 days after the last double-blind dose of the period.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard scales; MADRS with a structured interview guide. Who the raters were, and whether they were kept apart from dosing sessions, is not described in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit = a larger least-squares mean fall in MADRS from the period baseline to day 8 than on placebo (ANCOVA: period 1 with treatment and country as factors and baseline MADRS as covariate; period 2 adding the QIDS-SR16 stratum), the periods combined by a weighted test; dose-response by the multiple comparison procedure–modelling method (Methods › Efficacy End Points and Analyses).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None described for the three dose-against-placebo comparisons at each time point or for the secondary outcomes; the dose-response test used the multiple comparison procedure–modelling method. The sample size assumed an overall one-sided significance level of .05, and every printed P value matches a one-sided test (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind, with a bittering agent added to placebo and an identical process before period 2 for everyone, rerandomized or not (Methods › Design and Study Drug and Administration). No check of what participants or raters guessed is reported; the authors list difficulty blinding esketamine despite the bittering agent as a limitation (Discussion › Limitations).

analysis.effect_sizes: Period 1, day 8 (least-squares mean change, SE): placebo −4.9 (1.74); esketamine 28 mg −9.8 (2.72), 56 mg −12.4 (2.66), 84 mg −15.3 (2.56); differences from placebo −5.0 (2.99), P = .05; −7.6 (2.91), P = .006; −10.5 (2.79), P < .001. Period 1 at 24 hours: differences −9.1 (3.08), −10.0 (3.00), −10.7 (2.88). Period 2, day 15: differences −3.1 (2.99), P = .15; −4.4 (3.06), P = .08; −6.9 (3.41), P = .03. Periods combined: −4.2 (2.09), 90% CI −7.67 to −0.79, P = .02; −6.3 (2.07), −9.71 to −2.88, P = .001; −9.0 (2.13), −12.53 to −5.52, P < .001; dose-response P < .001. Editors' calculation: 95% CIs −8.3 to −0.1, −10.4 to −2.2 and −13.2 to −4.8; the printed P values are one-sided, the two-sided equivalents being about .04, .002 and < .001. Period-1 response at day 8: placebo 2 of 33 (6%); 28 mg 1 of 11 (9%), 56 mg 2 of 11 (18%), 84 mg 5 of 12 (42%); remission 1 (3%), 1 (9%), 1 (9%), 3 (25%). No standardized effect sizes are reported.
analysis.covariates: Period 1: country and baseline MADRS; period 2: country, period-2 QIDS-SR16 stratum (moderate or severe) and period-2 baseline MADRS (Methods › Efficacy End Points and Analyses, 1st paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01998958 (SYNAPSE), first submitted 25 November 2013 and posted 3 December 2013, before the January 2014 start. Version 1 names as primary outcome the change from baseline to the 1-week end point in MADRS total score, over day 1 to day 8 and day 8 to day 15, which matches the article's primary end point; the headline combined weighted test is described in the article's sample-size section. Version 1 planned about 60 participants with an open-label phase to day 25 and no panels; later versions added panel B (esketamine 14 and 56 mg, with sites in Japan; registry enrolment 108) and extended the open-label phase to day 74. This article reports panel A only. The protocol (Supplement 2) and eAppendix were not read. Read from the registry record and its version 1, not from the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: Panel B of the registered study is not reported in this article. Demographics by arm, double-blind adverse-event counts (eTable 4), CGI-S and GAD-7 results, blood-pressure and CADSS time courses (eFigures 2 to 4) are only in Supplement 1, not read; the statements that dissociation, dizziness and headache were more than twice as frequent on esketamine depend on it. Figures 1 to 3 are images whose values were not extracted. The handling of missing day-8 values is not described in the main text.
analysis.power: 60 randomized 3:1:1:1 gave 92.5% power for the combined day-8 and day-15 data, with an overall one-sided significance level of .05, SD 10 and 5% dropout, assuming differences of 9 points in period 1 and 7 or 9 points in period 2 (Methods › Sample Size Determination); 67 were randomized. The combined differences for 28 and 56 mg (−4.2 and −6.3) are smaller than the assumed effects.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After 1 week of twice-weekly sprays added to an oral antidepressant, MADRS fell more on each esketamine dose than on placebo in period 1 (by 9.8, 12.4 and 15.3 points against 4.9), with larger differences at 2 and 24 hours; in the small rerandomized period-2 groups only 84 mg differed significantly. Combined across periods the differences were 4.2, 6.3 and 9.0 points, with one-sided P values. On day 8 of period 1, 42% met response criteria on 84 mg against 6% on placebo, and fewer on 28 and 56 mg. In the uncontrolled open-label phase 22 of the 34 assessed at day 74 met response criteria, and at week 8 of follow-up 23 of the 41 assessed. Dizziness, headache and dissociation were more than twice as frequent on esketamine; blood pressure rose after dosing (maximum mean rise 19.0/10.3 mm Hg; highest values 199/115 mm Hg).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points and abstract say improvement appeared to be sustained with less frequent dosing for up to 9 weeks and that response appeared to persist for more than 2 months (Key Points › Findings; Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance); these rest on open-label and follow-up data without a control group, in those still present, all taking an oral antidepressant, so persistence cannot be attributed to esketamine. The Conclusions cite “evidence of robust and durable efficacy in the double-blind treatment phase”, which lasted 2 weeks. The Discussion compares the 1-week difference with 6- to 8-week differences in antidepressant trials in the FDA database, a cross-trial comparison (1st paragraph), and calls the doses apparently safe with no new or unexpected concerns from 56 people treated double-blind for at most 2 weeks (4th paragraph). The abstract does not say that its P values are one-sided. The authors acknowledge the small sample, the exclusions and the difficulty of blinding (Discussion › Limitations).

timeline.event: Zarate et al.: intravenous racemic ketamine 0.5 mg/kg against saline, crossover, 18 inpatients; Jaskaran B. Singh and Husseini K. Manji, authors here, were among its NIMH authors.
Murrough et al.: intravenous racemic ketamine against midazolam, 72 analysed; MADRS 7.95 points lower at 24 hours, no significant difference at day 7.

Singh et al.: double-blind, double-randomization trial of intravenous esketamine in treatment-resistant depression, with authors in common with this trial (Singh, Fedgchin, Daly, per the reference list); cited here for a rapid onset after intravenous esketamine (not read).
This trial, with a linked commentary in the same issue (doi 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2017.3738, not read).
Popova et al. (TRANSFORM-2): phase 3 trial of flexibly dosed esketamine nasal spray with a newly started oral antidepressant, on the Tier A list; not readable in this round (publisher check page).

replication.where_it_stands: Replication status is not judged on this card. This was the first trial of the nasal spray; its rapid differences are in line with trials of intravenous racemic ketamine read in this round (Zarate et al., 2006; Murrough et al., 2013), but whether the phase 2 differences held in the phase 3 trials could not be checked: Popova et al. (2019) could not be read, and the critiques on the Tier A list (Turner, 2019; Schatzberg, 2019; Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021) were not read.

funding.funder: Funded by Janssen Research & Development, LLC. Role of the funder as printed: employees of the sponsor were involved in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis and interpretation of the data; preparation, review or approval of the manuscript; and the decision to submit it for publication. Medical writing assistance by Sandra Norris, PharmD (Norris Communications Group LLC), compensated by Janssen; additional editorial support by Ellen Baum, PhD (Janssen) (Article notes › Funding/Support, Role of the Funder/Sponsor, Additional Contributions).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (Article notes › Conflict of Interest Disclosures): Drs Daly, Singh, Fedgchin, Cooper, Lim, Van Nueten, Manji and Drevets are employees of Janssen Research & Development, LLC and hold company stock or stock options; Dr Manji holds a patent assigned to Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Yale University and the National Institutes of Health, from which no financial benefit was received; Drs Shelton, Thase and Winokur report no conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: Eight of the 11 authors are Janssen employees (Titusville, San Diego, Spring House and Beerse); the others are at the University of Alabama School of Medicine (Shelton), the Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania (Thase) and the Institute of Living, Hartford, and UConn Health (Winokur). Daly and Singh had full access to the data; statistical analysis by Singh, Cooper and Lim, all Janssen employees. Esketamine nasal spray is the sponsor's product in development. Singh and Manji are also authors of Zarate et al. (2006), written at NIMH. The investigators thanked by name received no financial compensation for the acknowledgment (Article notes › Author Contributions, Additional Contributions).

what_would_settle_it: A large, pre-registered trial run and analysed independently of the manufacturer, with a randomized controlled phase long enough to test whether benefit lasts (including a randomized withdrawal), an active placebo or at least a recorded check of what participants and raters guessed, two-sided analyses, follow-up of every randomized participant, and absolute response and remission rates per arm at fixed times.

domains.note: Computer-generated schedules with randomly permuted blocks stratified by centre, but allocation concealment is not described (protocol not read). Period-1 baseline MADRS ranged from 31.3 to 35.0 across arms, adjusted for in the ANCOVA; other baseline data are only in the supplement.
Double-blind dosing with the oral antidepressant unchanged; analysis sets include everyone dosed with a baseline and at least one later MADRS in each period.

Day-8 data were missing for few people in period 1 (63 of 67 completed), but how missing values entered the ANCOVA is not stated, the groups are small (11 or 12 per dose; 5 to 9 in period 2) so a few missing values matter, and dropouts by arm are only in an image. The open-label and follow-up results describe only those still present.

An inert placebo with a bittering agent cannot mimic esketamine's dose-related dissociation, dizziness and other acute effects; no check of blinding is reported, raters are not described as kept apart from dosing sessions, the outcome is an interview about subjective symptoms, and the authors themselves name the difficulty of blinding as a limitation.

Prospectively registered with a primary end point matching the article, but the headline is a combined weighted test of the two periods, panel B of the registered study is not reported here, and the article does not say that its P values are one-sided.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized period-1 comparison of three doses against placebo, with a dose-ordered result and a prospectively registered primary end point, is reasonable evidence that esketamine nasal spray added to an oral antidepressant lowers MADRS scores over 1 week. The overall judgment is high because an inert placebo could not conceal esketamine's acute effects and blinding was not checked, so expectation may have enlarged the difference on a subjective outcome; the groups are small, the P values one-sided, and the sponsor took part in analysis and writing. The source can be cited for the size of the 1-week MADRS differences by dose, response and remission counts by arm in period 1, and the frequency of blood-pressure rises, dissociation and stopping for adverse events over 2 weeks; it cannot be cited for durable or maintained benefit, which rests on uncontrolled open-label and follow-up data, or for long-term safety.

key_findings.finding: 126 adults screened and 67 randomized in period 1: placebo 33, esketamine 28 mg 11, 56 mg 11, 84 mg 12. Of the 33 on placebo, 28 (85%) had a QIDS-SR16 of 11 or more at the end of period 1 and were rerandomized: placebo 6, 28 mg 8, 56 mg 9, 84 mg 5. 63 of 67 (94%) completed period 1 and 60 of 67 (90%) both double-blind periods; 57 entered the open-label phase, 51 (89%) the follow-up phase, 41 (80%) completed the week-8 follow-up visit.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Interventions; Results › Participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1, No. rows

key_findings.finding: Sample: 38 women; mean age 44.7 (SD 10.0); 43 (64%) with only 1 antidepressant failure in the current episode (plus 1 earlier), 15 (22%) with 2 and 9 (13%) with 3 or more; 26 (39%) had used an atypical antipsychotic as add-on treatment.

Primary end point, period 1 (day 1 to day 8; least-squares mean change, SE): placebo −4.9 (1.74), esketamine 28 mg −9.8 (2.72), 56 mg −12.4 (2.66), 84 mg −15.3 (2.56); differences from placebo −5.0 (2.99), P = .05; −7.6 (2.91), P = .006; −10.5 (2.79), P < .001. Baseline MADRS 35.0 (SD 5.18), 31.3 (3.80), 33.2 (6.26) and 35.0 (4.22).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Period 1, Change at study period end point; Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: P values are one-sided (editors' calculation; see reporting issues): two-sided about .09, .009 and < .001.

key_findings.finding: Period 1, earlier time points: at 2 hours after the first dose, differences from placebo −6.7 (SE 3.03), P = .02 (28 mg); −4.6 (2.96), P = .06 (56 mg); −7.9 (2.84), P = .003 (84 mg); at 24 hours −9.1 (3.08), P = .002; −10.0 (3.00), P < .001; −10.7 (2.88), P < .001. Placebo changes −9.7 (1.76) at 2 hours and −5.7 (1.79) at 24 hours.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Period 1, Change at 2 h and Change at 24 h

key_findings.finding: Period 2 (rerandomized placebo non-responders, day 8 to day 15): differences from placebo −3.1 (SE 2.99), P = .15 (28 mg); −4.4 (3.06), P = .08 (56 mg); −6.9 (3.41), P = .03 (84 mg); at 24 hours −4.8 (4.18), −6.1 (4.29) and −7.5 (4.77), P = .13, .09 and .07. Baseline MADRS 29.3, 31.3, 34.9 and 30.4 (placebo, 28, 56, 84 mg); groups of 6, 8, 9 and 5.

Periods combined (weighted test): differences from placebo −4.2 (SE 2.09), 90% CI −7.67 to −0.79, P = .02 (28 mg); −6.3 (2.07), −9.71 to −2.88, P = .001 (56 mg); −9.0 (2.13), −12.53 to −5.52, P < .001 (84 mg); ascending dose-response P < .001.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Periods 1 and 2 Combined; Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 95% CIs −8.3 to −0.1, −10.4 to −2.2 and −13.2 to −4.8; the printed P values match one-sided tests.

key_findings.finding: Response and remission in period 1 (placebo, 28, 56, 84 mg): at 2 hours, responders 6 (18%), 6 (55%), 4 (36%), 7 (58%); at 24 hours 1 (3%), 4 (36%), 3 (27.3%), 5 (42%); at day 8, 2 (6%), 1 (9%), 2 (18%), 5 (42%), with remitters (MADRS of 10 or less) 1 (3%), 1 (9%), 1 (9%), 3 (25%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Period 1, Responders and Remitters rows

key_findings.finding: Completers who had the same treatment in both double-blind periods, day 15: differences from placebo −6.0 (28 mg), −8.3 (56 mg) and −12.5 (84 mg); responders 3 of 8 (38%), 4 of 11 (36%) and 5 of 10 (50%) against 1 of 10 (10%) on placebo; remitters 1 of 8 (13%), 3 of 11 (27%) and 4 of 10 (40%) against 1 of 10 (10%).
key_findings.note: No SEs or tests are given for these completer comparisons.

key_findings.finding: Open-label phase (no control group): mean MADRS change from open-label baseline to day 74 −7.2 (SE 1.84). Response (50% or more below the period-1 baseline) at day 74 in 22 of the 34 assessed (65%) and at week 8 of follow-up, without esketamine, in 23 of the 41 assessed (56%); remission in 11 of 34 (32%) and 17 of 41 (42%) (by prior treatment sequence, placebo/placebo/open-label 6 of 6 and 5 of 7 responders; placebo/esketamine/open-label 5 of 10 and 3 of 12; esketamine/esketamine/open-label 11 of 18 and 15 of 22).
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph; Table 2 and footnote a
key_findings.note: Denominators are those present at each visit, not the 57 who entered the open-label phase; all continued their oral antidepressant.

key_findings.finding: Stopping for adverse events: 3 of 56 (5%) esketamine-treated participants in the double-blind phase, none on placebo, and 1 of 57 (2%) in the open-label phase (one event each of syncope, headache, dissociative syndrome and ectopic pregnancy). In the double-blind phase dizziness, headache and dissociative symptoms were the most common treatment-emergent adverse events on esketamine, each more than twice as frequent as on placebo; dizziness and nausea showed a dose-response trend. No deaths.
key_findings.note: Double-blind counts by arm are in eTable 4, not read.

key_findings.finding: Open-label phase adverse events in more than 10% of 57: dizziness 22 (39%), dysgeusia 13 (23%), nausea 9 (16%), headache 8 (14%), sedation 6 (11%); 14 of 57 (25%) reported transient dissociative symptoms; most dosing-day events were transient and mild or moderate.

Blood pressure and heart rate on dosing days: most esketamine-treated participants had transient rises, maximum mean change systolic 19.0 mm Hg, diastolic 10.3 mm Hg and heart rate 9.4 beats/min; the highest values (systolic 199, diastolic 115 mm Hg) mostly at 10 or 40 minutes after the dose, usually back to the pre-dose value by 2 hours; no dose effect on heart rate, the largest mean rises in the 84-mg group.

Dissociative and perceptual symptoms (CADSS) began shortly after dosing, peaked at about 30 to 40 minutes, resolved by 2 hours and became weaker with repeated dosing in all dose groups; no participant had symptoms suggesting psychosis on the BPRS positive subscale. The Discussion adds that these symptoms were dose dependent while the antidepressant effect did not weaken with repeated doses.
key_findings.note: The time course is in eFigure 4, not read; the Methods list CADSS ratings only before the dose and at 40 minutes and 2 hours (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Sample-size plan: 60 randomized (30 placebo, 10 per dose) for 92.5% power on the combined day-8 and day-15 data, with an overall one-sided significance level of .05, SD 10 and 5% dropout, assuming 9-point (period 1) and 7- or 9-point (period 2) differences and 40% moderate and 55% severe QIDS-SR16 scores among placebo-treated participants at the end of period 1.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Sample Size Determination, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Registration: NCT01998958 first submitted 25 November 2013, posted 3 December 2013; version 1 primary outcome, change from baseline to the 1-week end point in MADRS total score (day 1 to day 8 and day 8 to day 15), with about 60 participants planned; the current record covers panels A and B (14, 28, 56 and 84 mg; sites in the USA, Belgium and Japan) with 108 enrolled.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01998958: Study Details (current record) and Record History, version 1 (2013-11-25)
key_findings.note: Read from the registry, not from the article; the article states that it reports panel A (Methods › Design, 1st paragraph).

reporting_issues.issue: Every P value in Table 1 and the abstract corresponds to a one-sided test: for example the combined 28-mg difference −4.2 (SE 2.09) gives z = −2.01, one-sided P = .022 (printed .02) against two-sided P = .045, and the period-1 day-8 28-mg difference −5.0 (2.99) gives one-sided P = .047 (printed .05) against two-sided .094 (editors' calculation). The results never say the tests are one-sided; only the sample-size section mentions an overall one-sided significance level of .05, and the combined estimates carry 90% rather than 95% intervals.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1; Abstract › Results; Methods › Sample Size Determination, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers used to two-sided tests will overrate the evidence; claims should give the differences with the editors' 95% intervals (28 mg −8.3 to −0.1; 56 mg −10.4 to −2.2; 84 mg −13.2 to −4.8) rather than the printed P values.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the combined-period test statistics as −2.02, −3.04 and 4.24; the 84-mg statistic has the wrong sign for a difference of −9.0.

In period 2 at 2 hours, the 56-mg difference from placebo is printed as −4 (SE 3.92), but the group's least-squares mean change (−11.7) minus the placebo change (−6.8) is −4.9, which with that SE matches the printed P = .11 (editors' calculation); every other difference in Table 1 equals its two changes within rounding.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1, Period 2, Change at 2 h)
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed −4 is probably −4.9 truncated; use −4.9 with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 is titled as response and remission for participants who completed the open-label and follow-up phases, but its group sizes (10, 20, 27; 57) are everyone who entered the open-label phase, while its percentages use those present at each visit (34 at day 74, 41 at week 8), so 6 of 6 is shown as 100% for a group of 10. Two percentages are rounded up: 10 of 22 printed 46% (45.5%) and 17 of 41 printed 42% (41.5%) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The open-label and follow-up rates are observed-case rates among those who stayed, and should not be read as rates among all who started open-label treatment.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods schedule vital signs, CADSS and BPRS ratings only before the dose and at 40 minutes and 2 hours after it, but the Results describe blood-pressure maxima at 10 or 40 minutes and dissociative symptoms that began shortly after dosing and peaked at about 30 to 40 minutes.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Safety Assessments; Results › Safety, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs)
reporting_issues.consequence: The timing statements rest on measurement times not described in the article (perhaps in the protocol); the peak timing of dissociation and blood pressure should be cited with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The strength of the active spray is printed as esketamine hydrochloride 16.14 without a unit (14 mg of esketamine base per 100-μL spray), and the sentence giving 14 of 57 (25%) with transient dissociative symptoms follows the open-label results under the word overall, leaving unclear whether it covers the open-label phase or the whole study.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Study Drug and Administration, 1st paragraph; Results › Safety, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 25% should be cited as an open-label figure only with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that the two higher nasal doses give plasma esketamine levels in the range reached by an intravenous esketamine dose in earlier work, but no pharmacokinetic data are presented in this article.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not evidence for blood levels or for any comparison between routes; it must not be used as such.

reporting_issues.issue: The registered SYNAPSE study had a second panel (esketamine 14 and 56 mg, with sites in Japan; registry enrolment 108 against 67 here) that this article does not report.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01998958) and PMC HTML (Methods › Design, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The article is not the full record of the registered study; panel B results would have to be sought in the registry.
